body_text: Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory Reports Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results July 14, 2026 4:05pm EDT Download as PDF Related Documents 10-Q Filing PDF HTML XBRL ZIP DURANGO, Colo., July 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. (Nasdaq: RMCF) (the “Company” or “RMCF”), America’s Chocolatier® since 1981, is reporting financial and operating results for its first quarter fiscal 2027, which ended May 31, 2026. “Since stepping into the Interim CEO role, I have been encouraged by the commitment of our team, the engagement of our franchisees and the support of our Board,” said Allen Harper, Interim CEO. “I want to thank Jeff for his leadership and recognize the work he, Carrie and the broader team have done to strengthen the foundation of the business, including the important progress made across pricing, production efficiency, ERP and store-level systems, franchisee ordering capabilities and customer engagement. While our first quarter results reflect continued near-term challenges, I believe we are entering a phase where execution, alignment and accountability will be critical." “Working closely with the Board and leadership team, our immediate focus is on improving production, strengthening fulfillment and distribution, pursuing higher-margin product opportunities and evaluating ways to address the Company’s debt structure and working capital at favorable terms. These priorities will guide us in the coming quarters as we focus on product quality, service and franchisee support to better position Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory for sustainable growth. Most importantly, we want our employees, franchisees and customers to feel renewed energy around this brand. We are working hard to ultimately make chocolate fun again.” Mel Keating, chairman of the Board, added, “Al brings decades of leadership experience in consumer-facing businesses and a deep connection to the city of Durango, its people and this Company through his service on the Board and as one of the Company’s largest shareholders. His familiarity with our business, franchise network and strategic priorities allows him to lead from day one as the Company remains focused on disciplined execution and long-term value creation for shareholders.” Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results vs. Fiscal First Quarter 2026 Total revenue was $6.1 million for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $6.4 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. A 3% increase in Durango product and retail sales from price increases was offset by lower royalty and marketing fees under revised franchise agreements. Total product and retail gross profit was $0.2 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $0.3 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, reflecting lower packaged product sales. Total costs and expenses were $7.1 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, up from $6.5 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. The increase was driven by higher cost of sales, higher general and administrative costs tied to the franchise website and third-party delivery platform rollout, and higher retail operating costs with the increase from two to four company-owned stores, partially offset by lower franchise and sales and marketing costs. Net loss was $1.2 million or $(0.12) per share for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared to a net loss of $0.3 million or $(0.04) per share in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. EBITDA was $(0.6) million in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 compared to $0.2 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026. The Company will not host a conference call in connection with this earnings release. The Company currently expects to host a conference call in connection with its fiscal second quarter 2027 results. About Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory, Inc. is a leading franchisor of premium chocolate and confectionary retail store concept. As America’s Chocolatier®, the Company has been producing an extensive line of premium chocolates and other confectionery products, including gourmet caramel apples since 1981. Headquartered in Durango, Colorado, Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory is ranked among Entrepreneur’s Franchise 500® for 2026. The Company and its franchisees and licensees operate approximately 250 Rocky Mountain Chocolate stores across the United States, with several international locations. The Company's common stock is listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol "RMCF." title: 10 Key Steps in the Modern Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) Process to Know in 2026
summary: Learn 10 modern healthcare RCM processes to boost collections, reduce denials, prevent revenue leakage, and streamline your revenue cycle operations.
body_text: Modern healthcare organizations operate in an increasingly complex financial environment, where rising patient financial responsibility, stricter payer requirements, and automated insurance solutions make revenue management more challenging than ever. In clinics and hospitals, effective financial management is critical to maintaining stability, as even small inefficiencies can lead to significant revenue loss. Common challenges such as claim delays, denials, manual errors, and inaccurate data entry continue to disrupt the billing process and create revenue leakage across healthcare systems. These interlinked issues make it complex for healthcare organizations to sustain steady financial performance. This is where revenue cycle management (RCM) plays a vital role. RCM serves as an end-to-end solution that streamlines billing, coding, claims processing, and collections. It connects clinical services directly with financial outcomes, ensuring that every patient interaction is accurately captured and efficiently converted into revenue. Discover how leading revenue cycle management companies achieve comprehensive growth goals that go beyond costs and bottom lines. Download the e-book: 8 Proven Strategies for Growing your Revenue Cycle Management Company What is Revenue Cycle Management in Healthcare ? Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the end-to-end financial process that governs how healthcare providers capture, manage, and collect revenue for services delivered to patients. RCM covers the full patient financial journey, from the moment a patient schedules an appointment through registration, eligibility verification, clinical documentation, charge capture, coding, claim submission, payer adjudication, payment posting, denial management, and final patient balance collection. In healthcare practice, the revenue cycle is not a linear process but a connected financial solution where each stage impacts the next. Errors in early steps, such as patient registration or eligibility checks, can lead to claim denials, delays, and increased administrative costs later in the cycle. Revenue cycle management (RCM) plays a critical role in healthcare organizations by ensuring financial stability and operational efficiency. It is used across the industry, including hospitals, clinics, and solo or independent practices to manage reimbursements and maintain consistent cash flow. Revenue cycle management (RCM) is one of the most important aspects of healthcare operations, as it reduces inefficiencies, minimizes revenue leakage, and streamlines financial workflows to help healthcare providers maintain stronger financial performance and operational stability. Importance of Revenue Cycle Management ( R CM ) A well optimized revenue cycle management (RCM) process ensures: Stable and Predictable Cash Flow Reduced Revenue Leakage Across All Stages Improved Billing Accuracy and Compliance Alignment Lower Claim Denial Rates Increased Operational Efficiency Better Financial Transparency and Reporting Accuracy In modern healthcare systems, revenue cycle management (RCM) is the only option. It supports financial stability, improves operational efficiency, and helps organizations stay sustainable over the long term. 10 Key Steps in Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) Process 1. Patient Scheduling and Registration It is the fundamental stage of the revenue cycle management (RCM) process, where all insurance, demographic, and contact information are gathered before care delivery begins. This stage instantly influences the value of downstream billing results. Precise insurance validation, demographic precision, or patient identity are crucial because any discrepancy here propagates into delayed reimbursement or claim rejection in the cycle. From a financial perspective, patient scheduling and preregistration serve as the first checkpoint for protecting revenue integrity. Errors at this stage often lead to claim denials that require expensive rework or complete resubmission, increasing administrative cost per claim significantly. In 2026, leading organizations are increasingly relying on automated intake systems, real time data validation, and EHR integrated registration workflows to reduce human error. Within advanced revenue cycle management (RCM) solutions , patient registration is no longer a manual administrative task, but an automated verification process that ensures clean data flow into billing systems. 2. Insurance Eligibility Verification Insurance eligibility verification ensures that a patient’s coverage is active, and that services planned are reimbursable under their payer’s plan. This step has become financially critical due to the rise of high deductible health plans and more restrictive payer policies. When eligibility is not verified upfront, providers face higher rates of denied claims and increased patient responsibility balances. A failure in eligibility verification leads to immediate revenue disruption. Claims may be rejected due to inactive coverage, incorrect payer information, or unmet plan requirements. Modern healthcare billing workflow solutions now use real time eligibility checks integrated directly into scheduling and intake platforms. This reduces manual verification delays and improves first pass claim acceptance rates. Integrated platforms incorporate eligibility verification into the front end of the medical billing process, ensuring that financial risks are identified before services are delivered rather than after claims are submitted. 3. Charge Capture The process of documenting all billable clinical services delivered throughout patient care is referred to as charge capture. When clinical services are not properly captured, they end up in immediate revenue loss and cannot be billed. Today, charge capture failure is one of the major sources of unseen revenue leakage in healthcare ecosystems. Reimbursement per patient encounter can be reduced by missing procedures, delayed charge entry, or undocumented services. In 2026, automated charge capture systems are integrated with electronic health records (EHRs) to reduce dependency on manual data entry. These systems ensure that clinical documentation automatically translates into billable events, improving accuracy, and reducing missed revenue opportunities. 4. Medical Billing and Coding It is the procedure of transferring clinical documentation into consistent billing codes, for example, CPT, ICD-10, and HCPCS. Payer reimbursement completely relies on coding accuracy, which is why it is important. Claim denials, compliance audits, or underpayments can also be the result of these minor errors. Inaccurate coding not only delays reimbursement but can also trigger regulatory risk exposure under CMS and payer audit frameworks. As healthcare shifts toward value-based care models, coding accuracy is becoming even more important for quality-based reimbursement alignment. Modern RCM solutions that incorporate specialized medical coding services increasingly rely on AI-assisted coding validation tools to reduce human error, improve compliance, and support accurate claim submissions. 5. Claim Scrubbing and Submission Claim submission involves preparing and transmitting coded claims to insurance payers through electronic clearinghouses. This stage determines how quickly revenue enters the reimbursement pipeline. Clean, error free claims significantly improve payment speed and reduce rejection rates. Failures in claim submission often occur due to formatting errors, missing data fields, or mismatched coding structures. These errors delay processing and increase administrative workload. In 2026, automated claim scrubbing tools and EDI based submission systems are standard across advanced billing platforms . Integrated systems enhance submission accuracy by validating claims before transmission, reducing rejections, and improving first pass acceptance rates. Claim Rejection vs Claim Denial Aspect Claim Rejection Claim Denial Stage in workflow Front-end clearinghouse validation Post-adjudication payer decision Processing status Claim never enters payer system Claim processed but not paid Common causes Formatting errors, missing data, invalid codes Eligibility issues, coverage limits, medical necessity Correction effort Low (fix and resubmit clean claim) High (appeal or resubmission required) Revenue impact Delayed cash flow Direct revenue loss risk Industry RCM best practice Clean claim scrubbing before submission Denial prevention + automated denial management workflows 6. Claim Adjudication and Processing Claim adjudication is the process where insurance payers review submitted claims and determine approval, denial, or request additional information. This stage is heavily influenced by payer specific rules, contractual agreements, and regulatory requirements. The outcome of adjudication directly determines final reimbursement amounts. When claims are denied or partially approved, it increases downstream workload and delays revenue realization. Automation in adjudication prediction is becoming increasingly important in modern revenue cycle management process. Claim Adjudication Outcomes Outcome Meaning Revenue Impact Approved Claim accepted as submitted Full or partial reimbursement received Denied Claim not payable by payer Requires appeal or resubmission; revenue risk Pending / Additional Info Required Payer requests documentation Delays reimbursement cycle Partially Paid Only part of claim reimbursed Revenue gap requiring follow-up 7. Payment Posting Payment posting involves recording insurer and patient payments into the billing system and reconciling them with submitted claims. This step ensures financial transparency and accuracy in revenue reporting. Incorrect posting can lead to inaccurate financial statements and distorted revenue forecasting. Automation in payment posting, including electronic remittance advice processing, is widely used in modern systems to reduce manual reconciliation errors. 8. Denial Management Denial management is the stage where the platform identifies rejected or denied claims, finding out the root cause behind them and making sure they are accurate to be resubmitted. This is one of the most crucial stages out of them all, as it can slow down the reimbursement flow and increase the time to recover payments. The common reasons behind claim denials include coding errors, incorrect patient eligibility information, modifier or bundling issues, and missing prior authorizations. If not resolved in a timely manner, denials can increase administrative burden and accounts receivable (A/R) aging for billing teams. In modern revenue cycle management system, denial management workflows are often integrated with billing software to track denial patterns, flag recurring payer issues, and support faster claim correction and resubmission. This helps healthcare organizations reduce preventable denials and maintain more consistent reimbursement cycles. 9. Accounts Receivable Follow Up Accounts receivable (A/R) follow up focuses on tracking unpaid claims and ensuring timely reimbursement from payers. Delayed accounts receivable (A/R) cycles reduce cash flow stability and increase financial uncertainty. Organizations with poor account receivable (A/R) performance often struggle with liquidity issues even when revenue volume is high. Automation tools now prioritize aging claims, flag high risk accounts, and trigger escalation workflows to improve recovery timelines. 10. Patient Billing and Collections Patient billing and collections involve invoicing patients for remaining balances after insurance payments have been applied. With rising deductible plans, patient responsibility now represents a significant portion of healthcare revenue. Inefficient patient billing communication can lead to delayed payments and increased bad debt. Modern medical billing services use automated reminders, flexible payment plans, and digital billing portals to improve collection efficiency while enhancing the patient’s payment experience. Conclusion In 2026, modern RCM solutions run as an interlinked financial network where organizational stability and revenue integrity are directly influenced by each individual stage of RCM processes. Healthcare practices accomplish more powerful cash flow, enhanced financial predictability, and reduced administrative burden when patient access, claims processing, denial management, coding, and collections run as a single system. CareCloud’s platform supports providers to revamp the whole medical billing workflow, enhancing financial performance outcomes, minimizing inefficiencies with the help of unified workflows and automation. In an increasingly complex healthcare environment, effective RCM results in smoother operations, long-term sustainability, and better financial health. Frequently Asked Questions 1. How does automation improve the revenue cycle management process? Automation improves the revenue cycle management (RCM) process by reducing manual errors, enhancing eligibility verification, optimizing payment posting, speeding up claim processing, and supporting faster reimbursement cycles with increased operational efficiency. 2. What is the average revenue cycle timeline in healthcare? Typically, a healthcare revenue cycle timeline ranges between 30 to 60 days, and it may vary depending on denial rates, payer responsiveness, and claim complexity. 3. Why is RCM important for healthcare organizations? Revenue cycle management (RCM) is important because it helps healthcare organizations maintain stable cash flow, reduce revenue leakage, improve billing accuracy, strengthen financial visibility, and support long-term operational sustainability. 4. body_text: Jul 29, 2026 Ingevity reports second quarter 2026 financial results PRESS RELEASE Second Quarter 2026 Results and Recent Highlights: Net sales of $314.1 million decreased 5% from prior year; excluding Road Markings, sales increased 5% Net income from continuing operations of $39.8 million, or $1.13 per diluted share, compared to $(141.4) million, or $(3.87) per diluted share, in the prior year Adjusted earnings from continuing operations of $61.5 million and $1.74 of adjusted diluted earnings per share compared to $44.9 million and $1.22 in the prior year Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations of $115.0 million, up $14.0 million from the prior year; Adjusted EBITDA margin from continuing operations of 6% compared to 30.5% in the prior year Completed the sale of Road Markings product line on April 15, 2026, for approximately $63 million in net proceeds Raises full year Adjusted EBITDA outlook to a range of $380 to $400 million following a solid start to the year NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C., July 29, 2026 – Ingevity Corporation (NYSE: NGVT) today reported its financial results for the second quarter of 2026. The results and guidance in this release include non-GAAP financial measures; see “Use of non‑GAAP financial measures” section for definitions and reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measure. Unless otherwise stated, all comparisons below are made versus the same period in 2025 and are presented on a continuing operations basis. Full Company Results Net sales of $314.1 million decreased 5% driven primarily by the sale of the Road Markings product line on April 15, 2026. Excluding Road Markings, sales increased 5% with growth across all three segments. The company reported net income from continuing operations of $39.8 million or $1.13 per diluted share (EPS). Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) from continuing operations increased 14% to $115.0 million, driven by higher price, favorable product mix, and increased volumes in Performance Materials and Pavement Technologies, along with improved product mix and asset utilization in Advanced Polymer Technologies. Second quarter adjusted EBITDA margin from continuing operations was 36.6% compared to 30.5% in the prior year. “We are delivering on the commitments we set at the beginning of the year,” said Ingevity President and CEO Dave Li. “Strong commercial and operational execution across our businesses drove another strong quarter, giving us the confidence to raise our full-year diluted adjusted EPS and adjusted EBITDA guidance. While our outlook for the second half remains measured given the dynamic operating environment, our results reinforce the strength of the business and the progress we’re making in building a stronger, more focused Ingevity. The completion of the Road Markings divestiture in April further demonstrates our commitment to portfolio transformation. We also continue to invest in organic growth opportunities that leverage our differentiated carbon technologies. Our recent municipal water treatment contract for PFAS filtration provides early commercial validation of our technology and demonstrates its potential to create attractive new growth opportunities in adjacent markets. Together, these actions are creating a stronger Ingevity: a more focused company with differentiated technology, attractive organic growth opportunities, and a stronger foundation for sustainable long-term shareholder value.” Segment Results Performance Materials Performance Materials sales increased 4% to $160.6 million driven by higher volumes and favorable mix driven by a continued shift in consumer preferences from battery electric vehicles to hybrids, further supported by annual pricing actions. Segment EBITDA was up 6% to $86.1 million driven by higher volumes, improved price and mix, and higher plant utilization, which more than offset higher SG&A and other expenses. Segment EBITDA margin improved 100 basis points to 53.6% compared to 52.6% in the prior year. Pavement Technologies Pavement Technologies sales declined 22% to $104.2 million, primarily due to the April 15, 2026, divestiture of the Road Markings product line. Excluding the divestiture, sales increased 3%, driven by higher price and volumes with regional strength in North America partially offset by weakness in China and South America. Segment EBITDA was $25.4 million, down $3.4 million from the prior year, primarily reflecting the absence of $6.0 million of Road Markings EBITDA included in the prior-year period, partially offset by improved pricing and volumes in the remaining Pavement Technologies business. Segment EBITDA margin was 24.4%, compared with 21.4% in the prior year. Advanced Polymer Technologies Advanced Polymer Technologies sales increased 14% to $49.3 million driven primarily by higher prices, including a price surcharge to offset increased raw material and energy cost, a favorable mix toward higher-value derivative products, and competitor supply disruptions. Segment EBITDA for the quarter was $11.2 million compared to $2.0 million. The improvement was driven by improved product mix and higher plant utilization compared with the prior year period that included extended downtime associated with the installation of new boilers and further supported by competitor supply disruptions. Segment EBITDA margin was 22.7% compared to 4.6% in the prior year. Corporate and Other Corporate and other expenses, which are not included in segment financial results, were $7.7 million, similar to the prior year. Liquidity/Other Continuing and Discontinued Operations Second quarter operating cash flow was negative $15.8 million, a decrease of $120.2 million versus the same quarter in 2025 driven by a $113.2 million litigation settlement payment. Excluding the litigation settlement, the company generated $89.1 million free cash flow, an increase of $22.3 million. Second quarter of 2026 reflects improved earnings, reduced interest expense due to debt repayments, and lower restructuring spend compared to the prior year. Share repurchases totaled approximately $35 million for the second quarter at a weighted average cost per share of $70.94, with approximately $211 million available capacity remaining under the company’s current share repurchase authorization. Net leverage improved to 2.5 times versus the first quarter of 2026 and is down from 3.0 times versus the same quarter last year. Full Year 2026 Outlook: Following another strong quarter, the company is raising its full-year 2026 outlook while maintaining a measured view of the second half of the year. It now expects full year 2026 net sales between $1.05 billion and $1.15 billion, adjusted EBITDA between $380 million and $400 million, and diluted adjusted EPS of $5.00 to $5.45. Free cash flow is expected to be between $220 million and $245 million, excluding $113.2 million related to a litigation settlement. The company intends to utilize the strong free cash flow to reduce leverage to within our long-term target range of 2.0 to 2.5 times and return cash to shareholders. The 2026 outlook includes full year financial results for Advanced Polymer Technologies but excludes the divested Industrial Specialties product line for the full year and the Road Markings product line beginning April 15, 2026. Ingevity uses the following non-GAAP measures: Adjusted earnings (loss) from continuing operations is defined as net income (loss) from continuing operations plus restructuring and other (income) charges, net, goodwill impairment charges, long-lived asset impairment charge, acquisition and other-related (income) costs, pension and postretirement settlement and curtailment (income) charges, impairment of license agreement, debt refinancing fees, litigation charge, proxy contest charges, portfolio realignment costs, gain on sale of business, gain (loss) on strategic investment, and the income tax expense (benefit) on those items, less the provision (benefit) from certain discrete tax items. Diluted adjusted earnings (loss) from continuing operations per share is defined as diluted earnings (loss) from continuing operations per share plus restructuring and other (income) charges, net, per share, acquisition and other-related (income) costs per share, pension and postretirement settlement and curtailment (income) charges per share, impairment of license agreement per share, debt refinancing fees per share, litigation charge per share, proxy contest charges per share, portfolio realignment costs per share, gain on sale of business per share, gain (loss) on strategic investment per share, goodwill impairment charge per share, long-lived asset impairment charge and the income tax expense (benefit) per share on those items, less the provision (benefit) from certain discrete tax items per share. Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations is defined as net income (loss) from continuing operations plus interest expense, net, provision (benefit) for income taxes, depreciation, amortization, restructuring and other (income) charges, net, acquisition and other-related (income) costs, litigation charge, impairment of license agreement, proxy contest charges, portfolio realignment costs, gain on sale of business, gain (loss) on strategic investment, goodwill impairment charge, long-lived asset impairment charge and pension and postretirement settlement and curtailment (income) charges, net. Adjusted EBITDA from discontinued operations is defined as net income (loss) from discontinued operations plus interest expense, net, provision (benefit) for income taxes, depreciation, amortization, restructuring and other (income) charges, net, gain on sale of business. Total Adjusted EBITDA is defined as Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations and Adjusted EBITDA from discontinued operations. Adjusted EBITDA margin from continuing operations is defined as Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations divided by Net sales from continuing operations. Adjusted EBITDA margin from discontinued operations is defined as Adjusted EBITDA from discontinued operations divided by Net sales from discontinued operations. Total Adjusted EBITDA Margin is defined as Total Adjusted EBITDA divided by Total net sales. Total Net Sales is defined as Net sales from continuing operations and Net sales from discontinued operations. Net Debt is defined as the sum of notes payable, short-term debt, current maturities of long-term debt and long-term debt including finance lease obligations less the sum of cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash associated with our new market tax credit financing arrangement, and restricted investment associated with certain finance lease obligations, excluding the allowance for credit losses on held-to-maturity debt securities held within the restricted investment. Net Debt Ratio is defined as Net Debt divided by the last twelve months Total Adjusted EBITDA. Free Cash Flow is defined as the sum of net cash provided by (used in) the following items: operating activities less capital expenditures. Free Cash Flow per share is defined as Free Cash Flow divided by diluted weighted average common shares outstanding. Ingevity’s management also uses the above financial measures as the primary measures of profitability and liquidity of the business. In addition, Ingevity believes Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations and Adjusted EBITDA Margin from continuing operations are useful measures because they exclude the effects of financing and investment activities as well as non-operating activities. In questo articolo analizziamo la crescita della prima intelligenza artificiale generativa, OpenAI , e di altre due piattaforme straordinarie: Character.ai , che crea avatar virtuali per chattare e interagire, e il servizio di editing di video e foto facile da usare con diverse funzionalità intelligenti supportate dall'intelligenza artificiale, Wondershare.com . L’audience totale del suo sito, Openai.com , è cresciuta del 127% nel 2023, infatti a settembre 2023 il sito ha registrato 102,8 milioni di visitatori unici nel mondo. Sia lo strumento di progettazione digitale di OpenAI , DALL.E , sia il suo generatore gratuito di testo e codifica AI, ChatGPT , hanno stimolato la condivisione di contenuti e la sperimentazione sulle piattaforme dei social media. Per comprendere meglio l'impatto globale dell'IA, ci siamo concentrati sui dati relativi a otto nazioni. In Messico, il numero si è avvicinato al mezzo milione, seguito rispettivamente da Regno Unito, Brasile, Francia, Spagna, India e Italia. È interessante notare che l’analisi di questa piattaforma AI mostra anche un'elevata affinità nella fascia di età superiore ai 35 anni. Nel mercato del Regno Unito, gli utenti di Wondershare.com con età superiore ai 35 anni sono 1,26 volte di più della media internet in quella fascia d’età, anche in Messico l’indice (104) mostra valori più alti della media. L'IA generativa nel 2023 sta rapidamente trasformando il modo in cui creiamo contenuti, soprattutto per la generazione più giovane. Con l'evoluzione di questa tecnologia possiamo aspettarci che un numero ancora maggiore di persone abbracci questi strumenti nuovi e innovativi negli anni a venire. Per saperne di più, contattate Comscore o visitate il sito comscore.com/learnmore. body_text: View All News Speed Drives the Visit, Rewards Drive the Return, Vontier Survey Finds June 24, 2026 Download (opens in new window) New national research shows Americans are redefining convenience‑store loyalty around two expectations at once: faster, more seamless transactions and small rewards that deliver an immediate emotional payoff. RALEIGH, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- New national research from Vontier (NYSE: VNT) reveals Americans are quietly rewriting the rules of roadside retail. Consumers are reshaping the convenience-store visit in real time – demanding less friction and more value in the experience. New national research from Vontier shows Americans are redefining convenience‑store loyalty around two expectations: faster, more seamless transactions and small rewards that deliver an immediate emotional payoff. A survey of more than 600 U.S. drivers shows that nearly half (47%) of respondents want the ability to purchase snacks, beverages and everyday essentials directly at the fuel pump or EV charger. This marks the rise of Order at the Pump – the ‘Amazon‑ification’ of the forecourt, where every pump is expected to behave like a drive‑thru without the lane, the window or the wait. What used to be a quick errand is becoming a near‑instant interaction. But the story doesn’t end with speed. It begins with an interesting contradiction. Even as drivers look to bypass the store, they are not abandoning what the store provides. They want fewer steps, fewer delays and fewer interactions – but still expect the stop to feel rewarding, personal and worth returning to. Customers are separating the transaction from the experience and expecting both to be delivered in new ways. This duality builds directly on Vontier’s earlier research , which found that frequent visitors are motivated by identity – by feeling known, recognized and at home. The new findings show that identity and efficiency are not competing forces, but complementary expectations that C‑store operators must address. Today's consumers expect operators to cater to two distinct types of visits seamlessly: a fast, low ‑ interaction mode when they’re in a hurry, and a reward ‑ seeking mode where recognition and small perks matter. The operators who win will deliver both. Speed remains non-negotiable. Over 90% of drivers spend less than ten minutes on site, and 44% spend fewer than five. Reliability is equally decisive: seven in ten drivers say dependable payment and fueling systems are extremely important in determining where they return. Simultaneously, small, immediate rewards are rising in importance. More than half of drivers say free coffee or snacks make a loyalty program more appealing, with even stronger responses among Millennials and Gen Z. This dopamine perk signals that emotional rewards are becoming the new battleground for loyalty. Taken together, these trends point to a new model of convenience retail in which the forecourt becomes the primary interface for the entire visit: Transactions must be fast and nearly invisible; loyalty must feel instant, personal and emotionally rewarding; stops are becoming shorter; the car is becoming the checkout point; and the experience remains something customers want to return to. “Drivers are setting a new standard for routine stops,” said Mark Morelli, CEO of Vontier . “They expect the same speed and simplicity they get from digital experiences but still respond to the small details that make an in-store visit feel rewarding. The opportunity for retailers is to deliver both – fast, seamless transactions alongside experiences that customers actually look forward to.” The survey findings illustrate how these expectations are reshaping convenience store loyalty across visit behavior, transaction flow and rewards. Vontier’s portfolio of convenience retail and mobility technologies helps operators meet these expectations by connecting transactions, payments and loyalty across the forecourt and in‑store environment. By reducing friction at the pump and charger while enabling integrated rewards, Vontier solutions allow retailers to deliver faster visits without losing the elements that create repeat behavior. As convenience retail continues to evolve, the operators who succeed will be those who can resolve the central tension of the modern visit: making it shorter, simpler and more rewarding at the same time. title: Choosing the Right HVAC Contractor: Key Questions to Ask When Replacing Your Furnace
body_text: Replacing your home's furnace is a significant investment and choosing the right HVAC contractor is crucial to ensure a smooth and efficient installation. To help you navigate this process, here are essential questions to ask potential contractors. These inquiries not only ensure transparency but also help in building trust and understanding between you and the contractor. 1. Unexpected Delays and Additional Costs Question: What happens if something unexpected and time-consuming happens during the installation? Will you charge me extra? Why It's Important: No installation is immune to surprises, and it's essential to understand how these will be handled. This question helps clarify whether you might be facing additional costs if the project encounters unforeseen complications, such as the discovery of outdated wiring or other structural issues. A reliable contractor should provide a clear outline of their policy on unexpected issues, including how they handle extra charges. 2. Handling Permits and Inspections Question: What can go wrong during permit city inspections? Why It's Important: Permits and inspections are a critical part of the heat pump installation process, ensuring that the installation complies with local building codes and safety standards. Discussing this with your contractor can give you an idea of their familiarity with local regulations and their ability to navigate the bureaucratic aspects of the installation. 3. Incentives and Rebates Question: How do you help me with incentives? Why It's Important: Many local governments, states, and utility companies offer rebates and incentives for installing energy-efficient heat pumps. A knowledgeable contractor should be up-to-date on available offers and should assist you in applying for these incentives. 4. Sizing and Equipment Selection Question: How do you size and select equipment for my home? Why It's Important: Proper sizing and selection of your heat pump are vital for ensuring optimal performance and energy efficiency. An oversized or undersized unit can lead to increased wear and tear, higher utility bills, and a less comfortable home environment. A competent HVAC contractor should explain the process they use to determine the appropriate size for your heat pump based on factors such as square footage, the layout of your home, insulation levels, and climate. 5. Warranty and Service Guarantees Question: What kind of warranties and follow-up service do you offer? Why It's Important: Understanding the warranty on both the heat pump and the installation work is crucial. A good warranty will protect your investment, while a service guarantee offers peace of mind, knowing that the contractor stands behind their work. 6. Maintenance and Service Plans Question: Do you offer ongoing maintenance service plans? Why It's Important: Regular maintenance is key to ensuring the longevity and efficiency of your new heat pump. Some contractors offer service plans that include periodic checks and maintenance. Knowing these options up front can help you manage the long-term costs and performance of your heating and cooling system. 7. Licenses and Insurance Question: Are you licensed, bonded, and insured? Why It's Important: This is a fundamental question that ensures you are dealing with a reputable and legally compliant contractor. Licensing shows that the contractor meets certain industry standards, while insurance protects you from liability in the event of accidents or damage during the installation. 8. Energy Efficiency and Environmental Impact Question: What energy efficiency standards do the equipment you install meet? Why It's Important: With rising energy costs and increasing environmental awareness, ensuring your new heat pump meets at least the minimum government-recommended energy efficiency standards is crucial. This not only helps reduce your carbon footprint but also lowers your energy bills. Conclusion Selecting the right HVAC contractor is as crucial as choosing the heat pump itself. By asking these questions, you can gauge a contractor's experience, reliability, and customer service orientation. Remember, a good contractor will not only be willing to answer all your questions thoroughly but will also encourage you to ask them. This process is about ensuring your peace of mind and securing a comfortable, energy-efficient home for years to come.

title: Real-Time Insurance Verification: 71% of Practices Struggle
summary: 71% of dental practices say insurance verification is their #1 daily challenge. Discover how real-time AI verification cuts denials and boosts cash flow in 2026.
body_text: Why Real-Time Insurance Verification Is Breaking Dental Front Offices in 2026 If you asked 160+ dental billing professionals to name their single biggest daily operational headache, you might expect the answer to be claim denials, staffing shortages, or rising overhead. But according to the Group Dentistry Now 2026 RCM Report , the answer is none of the above. "Seventy-one percent pointed to insurance verification as their biggest daily challenge. Not collections. Not claim denials. Not staffing. Verification." — Foji.io, 2026 That number is striking — and it tells a story that every dental practice owner and office manager needs to hear. Insurance verification, a process that should be routine and predictable, has become the operational bottleneck that quietly undermines revenue cycles, strains front desk teams, and erodes patient trust. In this article, we'll break down exactly why manual verification is failing in 2026, what real-time automated verification actually looks like in practice, and how forward-thinking dental offices are using AI-powered tools to reclaim hours of lost productivity and dramatically improve their financial outcomes. The Manual Verification Problem: An Efficiency Paradox Front Desk Staff Are Drowning in Payer Complexity The traditional insurance verification workflow — calling payer hotlines, logging into multiple portals, cross-referencing benefit summaries — was already labor-intensive five years ago. In 2026, it has become genuinely unsustainable. Payer networks have grown more complex, benefit structures have become more granular, and the volume of patients with multiple or changing insurance plans has increased substantially. Front office staff are spending significant portions of their day on hold or navigating clunky payer portals, only to retrieve information that may already be outdated by the time the patient arrives. The result: claim rejections, patient billing disputes, and a front desk team that is perpetually reactive rather than proactive. The "Efficiency Paradox" Is Running Out of Room The 2026 Dental RCM Trends report from Zentist describes this situation as an "Efficiency Paradox." A strong 63% of practices are still collecting 90% or more of what they're owed — but they're achieving that only through intensive manual labor, not through operational efficiency. The system is being held together by sheer human effort, and that effort has a ceiling. Meanwhile, 78% of dental practices report an increase in claim denials or payer scrutiny over the past 12 months . Every denial that stems from an eligibility error — wrong coverage dates, lapsed benefits, incorrect coordination of benefits — is a direct consequence of verification data that was incomplete or stale. And with 58% of dental practices now committing to automation , the gap between early adopters and manual-process holdouts is widening fast. The Hidden Cost of Getting It Wrong Beyond claim denials, inaccurate insurance verification creates a downstream cascade of problems: Patient billing disputes when out-of-pocket costs differ from what was communicated at check-in Treatment plan abandonment when patients feel blindsided by unexpected costs Staff burnout from repetitive, low-value administrative tasks Delayed cash flow as A/R days stretch out while billing teams chase corrections 31% of dental practice respondents in the 2026 RCM Report cited rising patient out-of-pocket costs as the single trend most likely to impact their business performance. When patients are paying more out of pocket, they need accurate cost estimates upfront — and that starts with accurate, real-time insurance data. What Real-Time Insurance Verification Actually Means API-Driven Eligibility Checks in Under Five Seconds Real-time insurance verification isn't just "faster manual verification." It's a fundamentally different approach. Modern AI-powered platforms use direct API connectivity to payer networks, pulling granular eligibility data — co-insurance percentages, frequency limits, coordination of benefits, procedure downgrades, telehealth vs. in-person coverage — in under five seconds, without a single portal login. According to My Billing Provider's 2026 Automated Insurance Verification analysis , automated real-time verification achieves a first-pass claim acceptance rate of 94–96% , compared to just 70–78% for manual verification. Average days in accounts receivable drop to under 25 days, versus 45+ days with manual workflows. Those aren't marginal improvements — they represent a fundamental shift in how revenue cycles perform. Leading AI verification platforms can verify an entire day's patient roster in under five seconds, with connectivity to 300+ payers, according to DoctorConnect's 2026 review of AI insurance verification tools . Some cloud-based platforms connect to 1,000+ payers, including Medicare and all 50 Medicaid programs, as detailed in 314e's comprehensive guide to the top 18 insurance eligibility verification software solutions in 2026 . Batch Verification vs. Real-Time Checks: Understanding the Difference There are two primary modes of automated verification that practices should understand: Batch verification : Run automatically 24–72 hours before appointments, checking the entire upcoming schedule at once. This gives front desk teams time to address any issues before the patient arrives. Real-time point-of-service checks : Triggered at check-in to confirm that coverage hasn't changed since the batch run. Particularly important for patients with employer-sponsored plans, where coverage can lapse mid-month. The best platforms combine both approaches — running batch checks in advance and enabling real-time confirmation at the point of care. This layered strategy virtually eliminates eligibility-related denials. What Data Gets Pulled — and Why It Matters One of the most significant advantages of real-time API-based verification over manual portal lookups is the depth and accuracy of the data retrieved . A comprehensive real-time verification pull typically includes: Active coverage status and effective dates Deductible amounts (individual and family) and amounts met year-to-date Co-pay and co-insurance percentages by procedure category Annual maximum benefits and amounts used Frequency limitations (e.g., bitewing X-rays, cleanings, crowns) Coordination of benefits for patients with dual coverage Waiting periods for major services Procedure-specific downgrades or exclusions This level of detail allows front desk teams to generate accurate patient cost estimates before the appointment — a capability that directly impacts case acceptance and patient satisfaction. The Patient Experience Dimension: Why Transparency Wins Upfront Cost Clarity Is Now a Competitive Differentiator Insurance verification isn't just an internal billing function — it has a direct impact on the patient experience and your practice's competitive positioning. According to GetProsper.ai's Real-Time Insurance Eligibility Verification Guide , 75% of patients say that knowing their out-of-pocket costs beforehand influences their choice of provider . That's a remarkable statistic. Three out of four patients are factoring cost transparency into their provider selection — and real-time insurance verification is the operational foundation that makes that transparency possible. Practices that can confidently tell a patient "your out-of-pocket for today's crown will be approximately $340" before the appointment begins are building trust that translates directly into loyalty and referrals. Reducing Billing Surprises That Damage Retention Nothing erodes patient trust faster than a bill that arrives weeks after an appointment for an amount significantly higher than what was discussed at check-in. These billing surprises are almost always rooted in inaccurate or incomplete insurance verification. When a practice verifies coverage in real time and communicates costs accurately upfront, it eliminates the most common source of patient complaints and disputes. This is also where real-time verification connects to downstream revenue cycle performance. When patients understand their financial responsibility before treatment, they're more likely to accept treatment plans, make payment arrangements proactively, and return for follow-up care. The AI Patient Sales Coordinator from Patientdesk.ai builds on this foundation — using accurate insurance data to support treatment plan follow-up and case acceptance conversations that convert more proposed treatment into completed care. Real-World Outcomes: What the Data Shows Denial Rates Cut in Half — or More The business case for real-time insurance verification is well-documented. GetProsper.ai's 2026 guide highlights a compelling example from an orthopedic practice that implemented real-time eligibility checks: its denial rate fell from 11% to just 4% , and average time-to-payment dropped from 45 days to 26 days . While this example comes from orthopedics, the mechanics are identical in dental — and the financial impact is proportionally significant. A practice billing $2 million annually that reduces its denial rate from 10% to 4% is recovering an additional $120,000 in revenue that would otherwise require costly rework or be written off entirely. First-Pass Acceptance Rates That Change the Math The difference between a 70–78% first-pass acceptance rate (manual) and a 94–96% rate (automated) isn't just an operational metric — it's a financial multiplier. Every claim that fails on first submission requires staff time to identify the error, correct it, resubmit, and follow up. That rework cycle typically adds 15–30 days to payment timelines and consumes front office capacity that could be directed toward patient-facing work. My Billing Provider's 2026 analysis confirms that practices using automated real-time verification consistently achieve A/R days under 25, compared to 45+ days for manual workflows. For a practice with $200,000 in monthly production, cutting A/R days from 45 to 25 means approximately $133,000 more in cash on hand at any given time — a meaningful improvement in financial stability and operational flexibility. Choosing the Right Real-Time Verification Solution Key Features to Evaluate Not all verification platforms are created equal. When verification data flows automatically into your practice management system, it enables a chain of downstream efficiencies: Automated patient cost estimates generated and communicated before the appointment Streamlined check-in with pre-verified coverage reducing front desk friction Faster claim submission with accurate eligibility data pre-populated Proactive denial prevention through eligibility alerts that trigger workflow corrections This is the vision behind Patientdesk.ai's real-time insurance verification and front desk automation features , which integrate directly with PMS platforms including Dentrix, Open Dental, and Eaglesoft to automate verification workflows alongside appointment scheduling, patient communication, and billing preparation. When a patient calls to schedule an appointment, an AI receptionist from Patientdesk.ai can capture insurance information at the time of booking and trigger an automated eligibility check — so by the time the appointment is confirmed, the practice already has verified coverage data in hand. This eliminates the common scenario where verification is rushed the morning of the appointment because the information wasn't collected or checked in advance. It also allows the front desk team to focus on the patient experience during check-in rather than scrambling to verify benefits in real time. title: Veru Announces Full Enrollment for Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Trial of Enobosarm and Semaglutide Combination for High Quality Weight Loss

body_text: Veru Announces Full Enrollment for Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Trial of Enobosarm and Semaglutide Combination for High Quality Weight Loss July 27, 2026 8:10am EDT Download as PDF -- Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial exceeds targeted full enrollment of 200 patients — -- Interim analysis results on track for calendar Q1 ‘27-- MIAMI, FL, July 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Veru Inc. (NASDAQ: VERU), a late clinical stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing innovative medicines for the treatment of cardiometabolic and inflammatory diseases, today announced the completion of enrollment in the Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical study to evaluate the effect of oral enobosarm 3 mg versus placebo on total body weight, fat mass, lean mass, physical function, bone mineral density and safety in ~200 older patients (age ≥ 65 years) who have obesity (BMI ≥ 35) and are initiating semaglutide treatment for weight reduction. The interim analysis results from the study are expected in the first quarter of calendar year 2027 with final topline clinical data expected in the fourth quarter of calendar year 2027. “We are extremely pleased to have expeditiously completed enrollment in the Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial, which marks an important milestone in the development of enobosarm as a potential next generation combination therapy with GLP-1 receptor agonists for older patients with obesity,” said Mitchell Steiner, M.D., Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer of Veru Inc. “There remains a significant unmet medical need in older patients with obesity who are more likely to have low muscle reserves to make weight reduction more tissue selective by maximizing fat loss while preserving lean mass, physical function, and bone mineral density for the highest quality weight reduction. Retaining muscle and preserving physical function burns more fat potentially enabling patients to break through the weight loss plateau to have greater weight reduction.” Dr. Steiner added: “Achieving greater than full enrollment across the study sites reflects the dedication of patients, investigators, healthcare professionals, and the Veru team. This accomplishment advances our mission to make the weight loss process as healthy as it can be, benefiting patients and making their lives better.” Veru Obesity Program: Evaluating enobosarm in combination with GLP-1 RA for higher quality weight reduction in older patients with obesity Fully Enrolled Phase 2b PLATEAU Clinical Study Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical trial is a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the effect of enobosarm 3mg on total body weight, fat mass, lean mass, physical function, bone mineral density and safety in approximately 200 older patients (age ≥ 65 years) who have obesity (BMI ≥ 35) and are initiating semaglutide treatment for weight reduction. The Phase 2b PLATEAU study is designed to assess the ability of enobosarm treatment to break through the weight loss plateau observed in patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 RA treatment by preserving muscle mass and physical function to achieve clinically meaningful incremental weight reduction by 68 weeks. The primary efficacy endpoint of the study is the percent change from baseline in total body weight at 68 weeks. The key secondary endpoints are total fat mass, total lean mass, physical function (stair climb test), mobility disability assessment, bone mineral density, and patient reported outcome questionnaires for physical function, HbA1c, and insulin resistance. Results of an interim analysis assessing lean body mass and fat mass as measured by DXA after subjects have completed 32 weeks is expected in the first quarter of calendar year 2027. Final topline clinical data is expected in the fourth quarter of calendar year 2027. In June 2026 Veru announced a clinical supply agreement with Novo Nordisk for its Phase 2b PLATEAU clinical study*. Please see the Company’s SEC Form 8-K dated June 2, 2026 for further details. Completed Phase 2b QUALITY Clinical Study The Phase 2b QUALITY clinical study is a positive multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, dose-finding clinical trial that evaluated the safety and efficacy of enobosarm 3 mg, enobosarm 6 mg, or placebo as a treatment to augment fat loss and to prevent muscle loss in 168 older patients (≥60 years of age) receiving semaglutide (Wegovy®**) for weight reduction. After the efficacy dose-finding portion of the Phase 2b QUALITY clinical trial was completed at 16 weeks, participants continued into a Phase 2b maintenance extension study where all patients discontinued semaglutide treatment, but continued receiving placebo, enobosarm 3 mg, or enobosarm 6 mg as monotherapy in a double-blind fashion for 12 weeks. The Phase 2b QUALITY and Maintenance Extension clinical trial was a positive study that demonstrated that enobosarm plus semaglutide preserved lean mass and physical function, and led to greater fat loss during the 16 week active weight loss period and enobosarm monotherapy prevented the regain of weight lost when the GLP-1 RA was discontinued. About Veru Inc. Veru is a late clinical stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing innovative medicines for the treatment of cardiometabolic and inflammatory diseases. The Company’s drug development program includes two late-stage novel small molecules, enobosarm and sabizabulin. Enobosarm, an oral selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM), is being developed as a next generation drug that makes weight reduction by GLP-1 RA drugs more tissue selective for loss of fat and preservation of lean mass to improve body composition and physical function which is expected to result in clinically meaningful incremental weight reduction versus GLP-1 RA therapy alone. Sabizabulin, a microtubule disruptor, is being developed for the treatment of chronic inflammation related to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
